This is a simple creative mode sd card.

The station is lost. Anyone still uninfected, get to the transport ship now - we launch in twenty minutes with or without a full manifest. Bring the vaccine crates and nothing else. We can rebuild everything but the cure. Move.

We never cleared the launchpad. Someone we thought was clean turned in the cargo hold and tore into the fuel lines before we could stop him. The ship came down hard on the regolith. If you are picking through this wreck, take the vaccine and go. Do not linger where the infected fell.

Our first analysis of the infection samples has revealed some interesting findings. The infection appears to be caused by a previously unknown pathogen. The parasite is a highly adaptable and resilient microorganism that can infect a wide range of hosts, including humans. It has a unique structure that allows it to evade the immune system and rapidly replicate within the host's cells. We are currently conducting further tests to understand its transmission methods, incubation period, and potential treatments. More updates will follow as we continue our research.

It appears that the infection can be cured by a vaccine derived from the parasite's own structure. We still need to find how to contain the parasite, but we think that honey could be a good candidate for that, as it has natural antimicrobial properties.

We now know for sure that the parasite can be contained by honey, but it looks like honey alone is not enough. Adding some blue liquid seems to be necessary to make the vaccine effective. We are currently testing different combinations of honey and the blue liquid to find the optimal formula for the vaccine. We are hopeful that we will soon have a viable vaccine that can be used to treat infected individuals and prevent the spread of the infection.

The latest tests have shown promising results. We have found that a combination of honey and the weird blue fluid can effectively contain the parasite into the vaccine. As weird as it sounds, it looks like the last ingredient we need to make the vaccine effective is a casus vitreus cluster. We now think that the vaccine recipe is complete, and we are preparing for the next phase of testing, which will involve administering the vaccine to infected subjects to evaluate its efficacy and safety. We are optimistic that this vaccine will be a crucial tool in our fight against the infection and will help us save countless lives.

The final recipe is now complete, it contain a specimen of the parasite, an honey bottle, the blue liquid and a casus vitreus cluster. We will now be able to produce the vaccine to protect ourself about the infection.

The object came down harder than the models predicted, punching a crater wide enough to swallow a launchpad. Strange thing is, the rock is warm to the touch days later. Command has flagged the site for recovery. I just want to know what could stay hot this long out here.

We cracked the meteorite open and found threads of something organic laced through the mineral. Not fossils. They move when the lamp warms them. Doctor Vey thinks they are dormant spores. If she is right, this rock did not just fall on us - it was carrying passengers.

Two handlers reported a rash after opening the core casing. By morning they weren't handlers anymore. The spores don't need soil - they need us. We are sealing the impact site and shipping every fragment to the Moon labs, far from Earth. May whoever studies them there be more careful than we were.

There is something at the bottom of the complex that the smaller parasites answer to. It has been feeding and growing since the first host walked down here, an evolved thing swollen with every colonist it took. The others bring it warmth. It does not move much. It does not need to - everything in these tunnels is already part of it.

I made the vaccine and I could not save a single one of them. So I am carrying the last doses down to the core myself. If the evolved host is where the infection is thickest, then that is where the cure has to reach. If you are hearing this, I failed and you have another chance. End it at the source. Burn it with honey and don't look back.

When the surface fell, the survivors dug down and sealed the deep lab behind us. It was supposed to be a refuge. Instead the parasite came with us in someone's blood, and now the tunnels are its garden. The walls breathe. Growth pods hang in the old storage halls, and every day there are more of them.

They do not eat the ones they take. They keep them. I have been locked in this cell for days while the changed ones watch through the bars, patient, waiting for me to turn on my own. There is a vaccine somewhere in the boss vault below. If you found this card, you can still reach it. I cannot.

Observations for anyone who comes after. The parasites hunt by warmth and sound, and they never travel far from their spawning pods - destroy the pod and you thin the swarm. They can infect villagers, hollowing them into Parasite Villagers that still ape the old trades. Honey burns them. Cold slows them. Do not let them touch bare skin.

The sphere was here long before we were. It is older than the regolith it sits on, seamless metal that our drills cannot scratch and our scanners cannot read. The colonists thought it was a monument. Now I wonder if it was a warning we were too late to understand.

The aliens who trade at the sphere's edge are not surprised by the parasite. When we showed them a sample they recoiled, then offered goods in exchange for keeping it far from them. They have seen this blight before, on other worlds it hollowed out. The meteor did not bring us a disease. It brought us their oldest enemy.

Life in the colony is quiet. We farm moon berries under the domes and trade with the researchers up at the station. Lately a few neighbors have come down with a strange fever - pale skin, aching joints, a far-off look. The clinic says it is just cabin sickness. I hope the clinic is right.

It was never cabin sickness. The fevered ones are changing - skin cracking, eyes gone dark, moving in that same slow way as the thing they found in the rock. My neighbor was a farmer yesterday. Today he is a parasite wearing my neighbor's face. I am barricading the door and writing this so someone knows what took us.

Effective immediately, this facility coordinates all quarantine operations for the Moon labs. Every fragment recovered from the impact site routes through us. Our mandate is simple: keep the spores off Earth and keep the researchers alive long enough to understand them. Failure is not an outcome we are provisioned for.

Command has cleared the full budget for the Moon vaccine program. Supply rockets are loaded with reagents, isolation gear, and the honey shipments Doctor Vey's team requested. Nobody down here understands why they want honey by the crate, but her results speak for themselves. Send it all up.

We lost the last Moon relay this morning. No distress call, no signal degradation - just silence, all at once. Command is drafting the order to halt further launches. If anyone ever reaches those outposts again: we did not abandon you. We simply could not follow you into the dark.

Automated telescope flagged the incoming body six hours before impact - not enough time to warn anyone. I've relayed the trajectory and spectral data to Earth Command. The readings don't match any known asteroid composition. Whatever this was, it wasn't just a rock drifting home.

This satellite is now a quarantine beacon. I am rebroadcasting Command's warning to every Moon outpost on a loop: do not open the recovered fragments without full isolation. If you are reading this from the surface, the message got through. I hope it got through in time.

The samples arrived intact and the isolation lab is running perfectly. Under the microscope the parasite is almost beautiful - branching filaments that reach toward warmth like roots toward water. We keep them cold and sedated. As long as the station stays cold, we are the ones in control.

Petrov cut his glove on a sample tray four days ago. He said it was nothing. Today he stopped answering, stopped blinking, and walked toward the airlock like something was calling him. We have him restrained in the medical bay. The parasite doesn't kill its host - it drives it. That is so much worse.

Breakthrough. A vaccine grown from the parasite's own filaments halts the spread, and honey - ordinary honey - smothers the spores on contact. Its antimicrobial sugars starve them. We are synthesizing doses as fast as the reactors allow. For the first time since the meteor, I believe we might actually win this.
